text: When the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples, encouraged them, and said farewell before setting out for Macedonia.
He traveled through that region, encouraging the believers at length, and then came to Greece,
where he stayed three months. Just as he was about to sail for Syria, the Jews formed a plot against him, so he decided to return by way of Macedonia.
Traveling with him were Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Berea; Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica; Gaius from Derbe; Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia.
These men went on ahead and waited for us at Troas.
We sailed from Philippi after the Festival of Unleavened Bread and joined them at Troas five days later, and there we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week we gathered to break bread, and Paul spoke to them. Since he intended to leave the next day, he kept on talking until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were gathered.
A young man named Eutychus, who was sitting in the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on. Overcome by sleep, he fell from the third story and was picked up dead.
But Paul went down, threw himself upon him, and took him in his arms. "Do not be alarmed," he said, "his life is in him."

versions.text: But Paul went down, threw himself upon him, and took him in his arms. "Do not be alarmed," he said, "he is alive."
versions.explanation: The Greek says literally "his life is in him," which is more vivid and preserves the idiom; "he is alive" flattens the wording and slightly weakens the sense of the narrative moment. The literal phrasing also reads well aloud.

text: Then he went back upstairs, broke the bread and ate, and talked with them a long while, until daybreak; then he left.
And they took the boy home alive, greatly comforted.
We went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, where we were to take Paul aboard. This was his arrangement, since he intended to go by land.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, we arrived the next day off Chios; the day after, we crossed over to Samos, and the following day we came to Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he would not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent word to Ephesus, summoning the elders of the church.
When they arrived, he said to them: "You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I set foot in Asia,
serving the Lord with all humility, with tears, and with the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews.
I held back nothing that was for your good, but proclaimed it to you and taught you publicly and from house to house,
testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus.
And now, bound by the Spirit, I am on my way to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there,
except that in city after city the Holy Spirit testifies to me that chains and afflictions await me.
But I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course and complete the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus: to testify to the gospel of God's grace.
And now I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again.
Therefore I declare to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all people,

versions.text: Therefore I declare to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all of you,
versions.explanation: πάντων is unqualified ("of all"), and the context (Paul's proclamation to Jews and Greeks alike, v. 21) suggests a broader reference than only the Ephesian elders. "Of all of you" narrows the statement more than the Greek warrants.

text: for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.

Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God, which he purchased with his own blood.[^1]

[^1]: Or "with the blood of his own Son"; the Greek phrase can be read either way.

versions.text: Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God, which he purchased with his own blood.
versions.explanation: The Greek construction ("the blood of his Own") is genuinely ambiguous and theologically significant. The main text can stand, but a brief footnote noting the alternative rendering would help the reader.

text: I know that after I am gone, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock.
Even from your own number men will rise up, speaking twisted things, to draw the disciples away after themselves.

versions.text: Even from your own number men will rise up and distort the truth in order to draw the disciples after themselves.
versions.explanation: "Distort the truth" adds an object ("the truth") not present in the Greek, which reads "speaking twisted/perverse things." The participial construction also keeps the rhythm of the warning.

text: So be on your guard, and remember that for three years, night and day, I never stopped warning each one of you with tears.
And now I commit you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you an inheritance among all who are sanctified.
I have coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands of mine provided for my own needs and for those who were with me.
In everything I showed you that by such hard work we must help the weak, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus, who himself said, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'"
When he had said this, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
They all wept loudly as they embraced Paul and kissed him,
grieving most of all over his words that they would never see his face again. Then they accompanied him to the ship.
